passage: The bus to the science fair was leaving in six minutes and Jahnavi's phone battery was at two percent. Rafiq had just won the second prize for his water-filter model, and his post was full of hearts. She tapped a heart too, fast, and it felt like nothing. She hated that. Someone honked. She typed quickly: "Rafiq, the way you explained the layers to the judges made me finally get it. I'm proud of you." She sent it just as the screen went black. Rafiq read it on the bus, ignoring the loud celebration around him, and looked up. He caught her eye and smiled, then held his phone up like a small trophy.

qa.q: What did Rafiq win?
qa.a: He won the second prize for his water-filter model.

qa.q: Why did Jahnavi feel a heart was not enough?
qa.a: She felt the quick heart was empty and wanted to show she truly noticed his explanation. Her rush before the battery died shows how much she wanted him to know.

qa.q: What could Jahnavi do if Rafiq does not reply?
qa.a: She could simply tell him in person that she meant it, and not worry that a reply is missing.

qa.q: How might Rafiq have felt reading the message among all the hearts?
qa.a: He may have felt truly seen, because the message named something specific he had done.

grounding: A teen adds a specific personal message to a quick heart, and the specific note means more.

passage: Mohit's cricket reel had three hundred hearts by dinner. Divyansh scrolled through them at his desk. Most were just a fire symbol or 'nice bro'. One was from a boy who never talked to Mohit at school, and yesterday that boy had asked to copy his homework. Divyansh wasn't sure that heart was warm. He thought about what he actually noticed: the low slow-motion catch at the end, the way Mohit had waited for the dust to settle. He typed, "Your last catch made me stop scrolling. That slow-mo was the best part." Later Mohit came to his flat and said, "Your comment was the one I read twice."

qa.q: How many hearts did Mohit's reel have by dinner?
qa.a: It had three hundred hearts by dinner.

qa.q: Why was Divyansh unsure about the heart from the boy who wanted homework?
qa.a: He suspected that heart might be a way of being friendly for a favour, since the boy had never talked to Mohit before and had just asked to copy homework. He could not be sure of the motive.

qa.q: What made Divyansh's comment stand out?
qa.a: It named a specific moment he really noticed, the slow-motion catch, so it felt personal rather than automatic.

qa.q: How might Mohit see the 300 hearts compared with one comment?
qa.a: Mohit may enjoy the hearts but take the one specific comment more seriously, since it shows someone paid attention.

grounding: Digital compliments are quick, so sincerity varies, and a specific personal message usually means more.

passage:
"Did you see? Forty-one likes on my painting," Kalyani said, sliding her phone across the canteen table.
Nilesh looked. "I liked it too."
"I know. Everyone did. You also liked Rohit's photo of a samosa."
Nilesh laughed. "Fair. Okay, so, forget the like."
"Forget it?"
"The painting. The rooftop one. The way you did the water tanks in orange at sunset, and that one kite stuck on the wire. I looked at that kite for ages. It made me think of our old building."
Kalyani went quiet. She picked up the phone and looked at her own painting again.
"Nobody said anything about the kite," she said.
"It's the best bit."
"Can you write that? Under the post. Like, actually write it?"
"Yes."
That evening the comment sat there under forty-one likes, and she screenshotted only that.

qa.q: How many likes did Kalyani's painting get?
qa.a: Forty-one likes.

qa.q: What was Kalyani feeling when Nilesh talked about the kite?
qa.a: She was quietly touched and pleased, because his specific words showed he had really looked, unlike the quick likes.

qa.q: Why did Nilesh's spoken compliment mean more than his like?
qa.a: A like cost him nothing and he gave them to everything, but describing the orange water tanks and the kite showed real attention.

qa.q: What would change if Nilesh had just said "nice"?
qa.a: Kalyani would likely have felt the same about it as about the forty-one likes, pleased for a second but not really seen.

grounding: The dialogue shows likes as quick, low-cost signals and a specific personal message carrying more sincere admiration.

passage:
When my poem went up on the school magazine page last year, I checked the counter every hour. It crossed two hundred likes by the weekend, and I felt amazing for about ten minutes each time I looked. Then it felt like nothing. I couldn't tell who had read it and who had just tapped.
On Monday, Gautam, who sits two rows behind me and has never spoken to me much, sent a message. It said: "Your line about Nani's hands smelling of cloves. My Dadi's hands were like that. I read it to my mother."
I read that message maybe thirty times. I still have it saved.
Now when someone's work moves me, I try to say one specific thing, even if it feels awkward. A heart is fine. A sentence is better.
- Salma

qa.q: How many likes did Salma's poem get by the weekend?
qa.a: It crossed two hundred likes by the weekend.

qa.q: What did Salma feel about the two hundred likes?
qa.a: Salma felt amazing briefly each time but then empty, not knowing who had actually read the poem.

qa.q: What could a reader learn from how Salma now responds to others' work?
qa.a: Saying one specific thing about what moved you shows real attention, which means more than a quick heart.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Gautam to send that message?
qa.a: It may have felt a little awkward to write to someone he rarely spoke to, but the poem reminded him of his Dadi and mattered enough to say so.

grounding: The account shows admiration expressed through many quick likes versus one specific personal message that meant far more.

passage:
Class blog notes - Lakshmi (English teacher), Class 10
This week I asked students to respond to each other's short stories on the class blog. Seema left a heart on all thirty-two stories within twenty minutes. When I asked, she smiled and said, "I want everyone to feel supported."
Her intention is clearly kind. But when I read the comments aloud, the stories with long, specific replies got the biggest reactions from their writers. One boy said, "The hearts are nice, but I don't know if anyone read it."
So on Thursday I asked each student to write one real comment: name a line you remember and why.
Seema chose Deepika's story and wrote four sentences about the ending. Deepika came up to her after class and thanked her in person, which I haven't seen happen with a heart.

qa.q: How many stories did Seema leave a heart on?
qa.a: Seema left a heart on all thirty-two stories.

qa.q: What does Seema's answer suggest about why she hearted every story?
qa.a: It suggests she felt warm and caring towards her classmates and wanted them to feel supported, not that she was careless.

qa.q: How did Lakshmi's Thursday activity help?
qa.a: Asking for one specific comment turned Seema's kind but quick hearts into words that showed she had read the story, which meant more to Deepika.

qa.q: How might the boy who spoke up see the hearts?
qa.a: He sees them as nice but uncertain, because a heart does not show whether anyone actually read his story.

grounding: The teacher's note shows quick digital hearts of varying sincerity and a specific personal comment carrying more admiration.

passage:
Sunday night
Irfan finally posted the kathak video, the one he's been practising in the society parking lot for weeks. I tapped the heart in about half a second, same as the 63 other people. Then I felt oddly guilty, like I'd clapped from the back of a hall. A heart costs nothing. I'd watched him fall on that spin at least ten times in the parking lot. So I wrote to him separately: "The spin at 0:41!!! You nailed the one you kept falling on. And your hands at the end looked just like your teacher's. So proud of you 😊" Took me ten minutes to send it, because it felt like too much. He replied in two: "Pooja. I've read this four times. Everyone else just liked it." Then a voice note of him doing a tiny victory thump on the floor. Hearts are nice. Words are better. Noting that down.

qa.q: At what point in the video was the spin?
qa.a: The spin Irfan nailed was at 0:41.

qa.q: Why did Pooja feel guilty after tapping the heart?
qa.a: The heart felt too easy, like clapping from the back of a hall, after watching Irfan fall on that spin so many times. There was also some nervousness, since the real message took ten minutes to send.

qa.q: What made Pooja's message land better than the like?
qa.a: It was specific, naming the spin at 0:41 and the hands at the end, and showed Pooja had really watched the practice, which a quick heart can't show. 😊

qa.q: How did the messages look to Irfan?
qa.a: Irfan read Pooja's message four times because everyone else just liked the video, so the specific words meant more than the count of hearts.

grounding: It shows a teenager expressing admiration first with a quick like and then with a specific personal message that means much more.
